comparator.name: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology
comparator.sourceNotes: The official pages give 60 EC each year. The first two years comprise all listed required courses (60 EC each); the third has 30 EC compulsory, including a 9-EC thesis and a separate 15-EC independent fieldwork project. For the remaining 30 EC this pathway uses the officially permitted course-choice option at Radboud or elsewhere; the alternative 18-EC work placement plus 12 EC courses is not combined with it. No named formal route is selected. The year-specific pages are indicative 2026–2027 information, not a guaranteed future cohort schedule.

alternatives.concept: A social and cultural inquiry route linking inequality, cultural meaning, colonial histories, global cooperation and qualitative research. Sociology, history, law and political science provide related perspectives, while UCR does not offer Radboud’s dedicated anthropology sequence or independent ethnographic fieldwork.

alternatives.concept: A route examining environmental change through social inequality, Indigenous history, ecological science, sustainability governance and environmental justice. Qualitative social research and media analysis retain the target’s concern with lived perspectives, while specialist anthropological fieldwork remains a Radboud strength.

alternatives.distinctnessRationale: This curriculum substitutes foundations in sustainability and ecology, conservation, Earth-system methods, environmental biogeochemistry and applied environmental research for the broad route’s political institutions, private law, gender history and cultural-media courses. These changes implement the target’s evidenced climate-justice and human–nature direction.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest feasible response combines cultural meaning, social inequality, global change and related social research. The climate-justice route shifts materially toward human–nature questions with ecological science and environmental governance; the pair differs by more than four courses. Migration and belonging are evidenced, but the current UCR catalogue cannot support a distinct 24-course programme on that direction without making law and politics courses stand in for specialist mobility and ethnographic study.

The selected UCR courses do not directly study kinship as a sustained anthropological subject.
A course in qualitative methods does not replace Radboud’s separately credited first-year research project.
The UCR statistics course is aligned to the subsequent statistics component; Radboud credits descriptive statistics separately.
UCR’s personal development course is shown elsewhere; this distinct socially engaged component has no direct credited match.
The selected methods course is qualitative but does not independently reproduce the participatory-methods component.
The selected UCR courses do not specifically study debt relations and financial behaviour.
Ethics is present in a UCR alternative, but it does not reproduce a philosophy-of-science course on knowledge and research.
The separate nine-credit participatory research project has no scheduled UCR fieldwork equivalent.
European political institutions provide context, but no included UCR course directly examines lived im/mobility and belonging at this scope.
A stand-alone literature review is not present as an independent credited UCR component.
The second socially engaged learning component is separate from UCR’s first-year PPD.
Radboud’s nine-credit bachelor thesis is required; UCR optional research is a comparison-only option.
Radboud requires fifteen credits of independent fieldwork, which the UCR schedules do not provide.
The thirty-credit Radboud free-choice space remains genuinely open and is not assigned invented courses.

notes.text: Radboud combines anthropology and development sociology with a specialist theory and methods sequence, independent fieldwork and a bachelor thesis. UCR can approach inequality, cultural meaning and human–nature relations through sociology, history, law, media and environmental study, but these courses do not constitute the full disciplinary fieldwork curriculum.
